ev.y_first_word.text.4: You said “mama” for the first time – loudly, for the whole yard to hear. For a week afterwards your mother told every neighbor about it.
ev.y_first_word.text.5: Your first word was “give.” Your mother sighed: apparently everyone in this house starts that way.
ev.y_first_word.text.6: You laughed out loud for the first time – at a hen strutting past the doorway. Your mother called the neighbors to watch, and the poor hen was chased back and forth until evening.
ev.y_first_word.text.7: Your first word was “no.” Your mother said that at least now she knew exactly who she was dealing with.
ev.y_first_word.text.8: You've learned to wave, and now you wave at everything – the water carrier, the dog, the empty road. Your mother waves along with you so that no one goes unanswered.
ev.y_first_word.text.9: You crawled over the threshold for the first time and froze, staring at the rain. Your mother found you soaked to the skin and perfectly happy.
ev.y_first_word.text.10: Your first word was the cry of the water carrier who passes under the window every morning. Your mother laughed till she cried, and now the water carrier bows to you like an old acquaintance.
ev.y_first_word.text.11: You've learned to hide under the blanket and pop out squealing. Your mother is frightened every single time – very convincingly, and very patiently.
ev.y_first_word.text.12: Your mother was singing a lullaby when you suddenly joined in – missing every note, but with all your heart. She had to finish the song through her laughter.
ev.y_first_word.text.13: For the first time you said your own name – so mangled that no one but your mother understood. She understood at once.
ev.y_first_word.text.14: You fed yourself for the first time – with your hands, your cheek and a bit of your ear. Washing you took your mother longer than the meal did, but she was very proud.
ev.y_first_word.text.15: You climbed to the very top of the steps, couldn't get down again, and started bawling. Your mother lifted you down and told the neighbor, “The stubbornness is mine.”
ev.y_first_word.text.16: You pointed at the hearth and said, very clearly, “Ow!” Your mother decided there could be no more sensible first word.
ev.y_first_word.text.17: For the first time you copied the bird outside the window – so well that it answered. Ever since, your mother has called you her little bird.
ev.y_first_word.text.18: You took five steps in a row – from the wall straight into your mother's arms. She hugged you so tight that you protested.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.1: A soaked puppy shivers under an awning – skinny, with one floppy ear. It looks at you as if it had been waiting for you all along.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.2: At the market a puppy sits under the fishmonger's stall, licking scales off the ground. The fishmonger kicks it away; it trots off three steps and sits down again – right at your feet.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.3: A puppy has been following you all the way from the well. You stop – it stops; you turn around – and it pretends to be looking at the sky.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.4: After the downpour a puppy is whimpering in the ditch: the sides are slippery and it can't climb out. You haul it up by the scruff – muddy, shivering – and it immediately licks your hands.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.5: A whole litter of puppies used to live in the abandoned shed at the end of the street. Now only one is left – the smallest, with a white spot on its forehead. It crawls out to meet you, squeaking.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.6: A puppy snatched the flatbread right out of your hand and bolted. A minute later it came back – no flatbread, but wagging its tail as though it had been a fair trade.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.7: In the midday heat a puppy lies in the shade of a wall, licking a paw it keeps tucked up. When you come near it tries to stand, then sits right back down.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.8: Early in the morning a puppy is curled up by the baker's cooling oven, warming itself on the stones. The baker threatens it with a broom, and the puppy just buries its nose deeper in its tail.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.9: The neighborhood boys have cornered a puppy and are pelting it with pebbles. You shouted at them and they scattered, and the puppy stayed put, staring at you with enormous eyes.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.10: A puppy sits by the roadside with a frayed bit of rope round its neck. It must have belonged to someone once – and now it belongs to no one. It doesn't bark or beg; it just waits.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.11: By the temple gate, where bread is handed out to the poor, a puppy is snuffling up crumbs. The watchman shoos it half-heartedly, and the puppy seems to have already chosen you.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.12: You were gathering firewood and left your basket under a tree. When you came back, a puppy was asleep in it, curled up among the sticks, with no intention of waking up.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.13: Travelers camped by the road and left at dawn, but their puppy stayed behind – either it got left behind or they abandoned it. All day it has sat in the same spot, looking the way they went.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.14: A spotted puppy is nosing about by the fence: one eye brown, the other blue. The old women say it's a bad omen, but you think there has never been a more beautiful dog.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.15: Down by the river a puppy is hunting frogs – and losing so far. Soaked to the ears, it scrambles up the bank, shakes itself all over you and sits down beside you like an old friend.
ev.y_stray_dog.text.16: All night something whimpered softly at your door. In the morning there was a puppy on the doorstep – skinny, filthy and, by the look of it, firmly resolved to move in.
ev.y_stray_dog.title.2: A Puppy by the Fish Stalls
ev.y_stray_dog.take_home.16: Let it in and beg your father
ev.infant_fever.text.1: One winter you fell gravely ill. Your mother sat by your bed for three nights. You survived, but stayed weak for a long time.
ev.infant_fever.text.2: In autumn you caught a cough – dry and barking, loud enough for the neighbors to hear through the wall. Your mother carried you in her arms all night, because lying down you couldn't breathe. By spring the cough was gone, but you stayed thin for a long time.
ev.infant_fever.text.3: In the worst of the heat you suddenly went limp and burned like a coal. Your mother wiped you with a wet cloth until morning and gave you water from her palm. The fever broke, but for a long time you stayed quiet and listless.
ev.infant_fever.text.4: You broke out in a red rash and tossed in fever for a week. Your mother hung a cloth over the doorway against prying eyes and let no one near you. The rash faded, leaving a couple of marks and a lingering weakness.
ev.infant_fever.text.5: Something you ate disagreed with you: you were sick for three days and wasted away before everyone's eyes. Your mother fed you broth drop by drop and didn't sleep a wink. You pulled through, but for a long time you would barely eat.
ev.infant_fever.text.6: Your ear began to ache, and you cried until you were hoarse. Your mother warmed salt in a rag, held it to your ear and sang until her own voice gave out. The pain retreated, and half your strength went with it.
ev.infant_fever.text.7: You were ill all winter – fever, then chills, then fever again. Your mother slept sitting up by your bed and covered you with everything the house had. In spring you got back on your feet, though unsteadily.
ev.infant_fever.text.8: One night you stopped crying and just breathed heavily. Your mother wrapped you in a shawl and ran with you to the old wise woman at the far end of the settlement. You came back at dawn – slowly, but together.
ev.infant_fever.text.9: Your teeth came in hard, with fever and delirium. Your mother rubbed your gums with honey and didn't put you down for a week. The teeth came through, but you were noticeably weaker.
ev.infant_fever.text.10: In the damp of spring you caught such a chill that you wheezed with every breath. Your mother kept you by the fire and changed the hot stones at your feet all night. You recovered, but for half a year you caught every illness going.
ev.infant_fever.text.11: A sickness was going round the street, and it didn't pass your house by. You lay flat for three days, and your mother never left your side, even when the neighbors told her to look after herself. You survived, though for a long time you were as weak as a kitten.
ev.infant_fever.text.12: Something stung you in the grass, and by evening your little leg had swollen and you were burning with fever. All night your mother held the swollen leg in cold water and whispered soft things to you. The swelling went down, but it took you a month to learn to walk again.
ev.infant_fever.text.13: In the middle of the night you woke burning with fever and didn't know anyone. Your mother prayed, wept and prayed again, holding you until dawn. By morning you knew her – and fell asleep. That night left you weak for a long time.
ev.infant_fever.text.14: Suddenly you stopped eating and just lay there, staring at the ceiling. For a week your mother fed you from her finger, crumb by crumb, soaked in warm broth. Your appetite came back; the color in your cheeks took much longer.
ev.infant_fever.text.15: That hot summer the well water went stale, and you were one of the first to fall ill. Your mother started fetching water from a distant spring and gave it to you sip by sip, day and night. You got up again, but for a long time you were as pale as a shadow.
ev.infant_fever.text.16: For a week you lay in fever and barely opened your eyes. Your mother sang you the same lullaby hundreds of times, until her voice cracked. You survived, thin as a reed, and for the rest of your life that tune sounded strangely familiar.
ev.infant_fever.title.8: A Night at the Wise Woman's
ev.marriage_f.text.1: Your family has arranged your marriage. That is the custom: girls marry young, and few ask what they think.
ev.marriage_f.text.2: Your family has found you a groom – a widower twice your age, but with a solid house and no debts. The betrothal has already been toasted without waiting for your word.
ev.marriage_f.text.3: For three days the matchmaker has been sitting in the house praising the groom: hard-working, sober, from a good family. Your family keeps nodding, and it occurs to no one to ask you.
ev.marriage_f.text.4: The groom lives in another town, several days' journey away. You've never laid eyes on him, but the dowry is already being packed, and your elders say you'll have plenty of time to look at him later.
ev.marriage_f.text.5: You've been promised to the boy next door – the one you used to pelt with mud as children. He's grown broad in the shoulders and blushes to the ears whenever he sees you. The wedding is set for autumn.
ev.marriage_f.text.6: A wealthy family has sent matchmakers, and your relatives can't believe their luck. The groom, they say, is sickly and spoiled, but a match like this can't be passed up – and the dowry will have to be a big one.
ev.marriage_f.text.7: The groom is a journeyman from the workshop down the street: calloused hands, kind eyes, few words. Your elders have already shaken on it and are discussing the dowry.
ev.marriage_f.text.8: Your family owes money to another family, and they've offered to forgive the debt – if you marry into their house. It was discussed behind a closed door, but the walls are thin.
ev.marriage_f.text.9: It turns out you were promised as a bride while still in the cradle – an agreement between old family friends. Now the groom has grown up, and his people are reminding yours of the deal.
ev.marriage_f.text.10: You haven't had your fill of being young yet, and your family has already agreed on the wedding. The groom is said to be a decent man – you just don't know him at all.
ev.marriage_f.text.11: A traveling merchant has been calling often – bringing a gift one day, sitting with the family the next. Yesterday he asked for your hand outright, and it seems no one said no.
ev.marriage_f.text.12: Today is the viewing: you've been dressed up, sat down and told to keep quiet. The groom and his people look you over like something at the market, and they seem satisfied.
ev.marriage_f.text.13: At the festival you danced with your friends, and a week later matchmakers came to the house – someone had noticed you. Your family is pleased: the groom is steady and his household prosperous.
ev.marriage_f.text.14: He's a good groom, your family says – only you'll have to live in his house, under the eye of a stern mother-in-law. Everyone sighs about it, but the wedding day is already set.
ev.marriage_f.text.15: The marriage is decided, and the whole house is busy with the dowry: counting cloth, pots, anything that can be given. You watch your future being packed into a chest, and nobody asks whether you want to go with it.
ev.marriage_f.text.16: The matchmakers came from that very boy you used to steal glances at by the well. Your family agrees – but suddenly you're frightened: it's all so fast, and there'll be no turning back.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.1: By the fire Grandmother told frightening and wonderful stories of heroes and monsters. You always fell asleep before the end and demanded the rest in the morning.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.1.polytheist: By the fire Grandmother told frightening and wonderful stories of gods and heroes. You always fell asleep before the end and demanded the rest in the morning.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.1.rome: By the fire Grandmother told the story of the twins Romulus and Remus, nursed by a she-wolf. Ever since, you have looked at every dog with respect.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.1.athens: By the fire Grandmother told how Theseus slew the Minotaur and found his way out of the labyrinth by a thread. The next day you wandered the courtyard with a ball of wool.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.1.egypt: By the fire Grandmother told how Isis searched the whole land for her husband Osiris and brought him back to life. You cried, even though you knew it would end well.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.2: Grandmother told the tale of a trickster who fooled a greedy rich man and gave his goods away to the poor. You laughed so hard that you were told three times to settle down and sleep.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.3: In a whisper, Grandmother told of a spirit that roams the crossroads at night asking passers-by for directions. For a month afterwards you went the long way round the crossroads – even in daylight.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.4: According to Grandmother, the stars are little lights that the souls of good people kindle in the sky. You sat on the doorstep a long time trying to find the brightest one.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.5: Grandmother told of a faraway land where people have dogs' heads and the rivers run with milk. You made up your mind that someday you would get there.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.6: Grandmother told the story of a girl who outwitted Death itself and bargained for another hundred years. You listened breathlessly and decided you could do it too.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.7: Grandmother told about the giant asleep under the far hill so vividly that the hill seemed alive to you. You even pressed your ear to the ground to listen to him snore.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.8: Grandmother explained why the moon has spots: long ago a curious little creature climbed up there and never came back down. Ever since, at every full moon you search for it.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.9: The tale was about a talking fish that granted wishes until the fisherman grew greedy. You spent a long time deciding what you would ask for – and settled on three wishes, no more.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.10: Grandmother told of a righteous man who shared his last crust with a beggar – and the beggar turned out to be a messenger from heaven. After that, you looked a little more closely at the beggars by the gate.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.11: Grandmother told how in the old days the river flooded right up to the mountains, and the only ones saved were those who listened to an old seer in time. You asked how to recognize a seer, and Grandmother said, “He usually grumbles.”
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.12: Grandmother's fable about talking animals ended with a moral, but you fell asleep at the best part – when the fox was dividing the spoils. In the morning she refused to repeat it: “Work out the moral yourself.”
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.13: Grandmother told of a girl who disguised herself as a warrior and saved her city. The next day you armed yourself with a stick and guarded the yard gate until evening.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.14: Grandmother had her own story of where fire came from: a little bird stole it from the thunderstorm and scorched its breast. Afterwards you kept peering at birds to see which one had a red spot.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.15: Grandmother told of a sage who lived in a cave and knew the answer to every question. The next morning you asked her forty questions in a row, and she said being a sage is hard work.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.16: During a storm, while the wind howled through the cracks, Grandmother explained that it was the spirits of the mountains and the plains arguing. You stopped being afraid of storms – now you just wanted to know who would win.
ev.y_grandma_tales.text.17: Grandmother told of a wise hermit who could talk with birds and beasts. The next morning you spent a solid hour trying to coax a sparrow onto your hand.
ev.y_swim.text.1: On a hot day you swam on your own for the first time – doggy-paddling, eyes bulging, but swimming!
ev.y_swim.text.1.rome: On a hot day you swam across a backwater of the Tiber for the first time. The old men say a Roman must know how to swim – how else will he cross rivers on campaign?
ev.y_swim.text.1.athens: On a hot day you swam on your own for the first time. In Athens they say of a dunce, 'He can neither swim nor read' – so you're halfway there.
ev.y_swim.text.1.egypt: On a hot day you swam in an irrigation canal for the first time, while the grown-ups kept a sharp eye on the reeds. Crocodiles are no joke.
ev.y_swim.text.2: The older kids shoved you off the planks into the millpond – and to everyone's surprise you didn't sink, you swam. You no longer felt like being angry with them.
ev.y_swim.text.3: You learned to swim in the shallows by the reeds, holding on to a bundle of rushes. A week later you didn't need the rushes.
ev.y_swim.text.4: For the first time you dived with your eyes open and saw a quiet green world under the water. You surfaced with a pebble in your fist and the feeling that you knew a great secret.
ev.y_swim.text.5: On a bet you swam across the stream and back, though only yesterday you were floundering by the bank. The prize – a handful of dried berries – felt like a king's reward.
ev.y_swim.text.6: You learned to swim in the pond alongside the ducks. The ducks seemed to consider you a very clumsy duck, but by the end of summer you could almost keep up.
ev.y_swim.text.7: An old fisherman showed you how to float on your back with your arms spread and look at the sky. You lay like that until you got cold, and it was the best thing that happened to you all summer.
ev.y_swim.text.8: You slipped on a wet stone and went headfirst into a deep pool. By the time you realized you were drowning, your arms and legs had already carried you to the bank on their own.
ev.y_swim.text.9: After the downpour a whole lake filled the ravine, and every kid around splashed there till dark. That's where you learned to swim – in murky, warm, absolutely perfect water.
ev.y_swim.text.10: For the first time you swam out to the snag in the middle of the river and sat on it like a throne until someone called you from the bank to come and eat.
ev.y_swim.text.11: You were afraid of deep water for a long time, then one day you just took a run and jumped. You came up shrieking and didn't get out of the water again until evening.
ev.y_swim.text.12: The wind blew your hat into the river, and to catch it you had to swim – so you did. You never caught the hat, but nobody minded.
ev.y_swim.text.13: The other kids taught you to swim frog-style, and you spent the whole day croaking with pride. Soaked and blue-lipped, but unbeatable.
ev.y_swim.text.14: The first time you swam was in a cold river early in spring – and you shot out onto the bank as if scalded. Still, now you can honestly say you swim.
ev.y_swim.text.15: For half the summer you just watched the older kids swim, then one day you walked into the water and swam as if you always could. Nobody believed you hadn't been practicing in secret.
ev.y_swim.text.16: For the first time you beat the neighbor's boy at swimming – the one who always swam best. He claimed he had water in his ears, but everyone saw.
ev.y_swim.text.17: At sunset the river water was as warm as fresh milk. You swam your first ten strokes and lay on the bank a long while afterwards, listening to your heart pound.
ev.y_nickname.text.4: They nicknamed you Grasshopper: you can't walk, only hop. You tried walking sedately – it lasted half a day.
ev.y_nickname.text.5: You follow the older kids everywhere, so they've nicknamed you Little Tail. It stung, but now they take you everywhere – who goes anywhere without their tail?
ev.y_nickname.text.6: For your loud voice they named you Crow. You cawed back at them – and the name stuck for good.
ev.y_nickname.text.7: You're quiet and easy to overlook, so the kids call you Mouse. Then again, at hide-and-seek nobody can find you – not even the grown-ups.
ev.y_nickname.text.8: They call you Mosquito: small, but nobody gets any peace from you. You've decided it's practically a compliment.
ev.y_nickname.text.9: For your stubbornness they named you Billy Goat. You stubbornly refused to answer to it – which only proved how well it fit.
ev.y_nickname.text.10: They call you Magpie: you hear all the street's news before anyone else and spread it even faster. The grown-ups now lower their voices when you're around.
ev.y_nickname.text.11: Your hair sticks out in every direction, so they've named you Hedgehog. However much you smooth it down, by midday you're a hedgehog again.
ev.y_nickname.text.12: You ask so many questions that they've nicknamed you Why-Why. You asked why – and everyone laughed.
ev.y_nickname.text.13: You fell into a puddle in front of the whole street, and ever since you've been Froggy. Frogs, you pointed out, are excellent jumpers.
ev.y_nickname.text.14: They named you Pebble: you don't cry when you fall, and you don't budge when pushed. You wear the name with pride.
ev.y_nickname.text.15: You're always muttering something under your breath, so they call you Bumblebee. You buzzed something rude back at them.
ev.y_nickname.text.16: You tried to walk as solemnly as an elder, so they nicknamed you {g:Grandpa|Granny}. You waved them off exactly like an old-timer – and everyone fell about laughing.
ev.y_nickname.text.17: Because you're forever climbing the tallest trees, they call you Birdie. The grown-ups grumble, but the kids come to you whenever something gets stuck in a branch.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.1: At the feast the host ordered the strongest drink poured, and every cup must be drained. Anyone who sips gets laughed at, and the cup goes round faster and faster.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.1.rome: At a rich neighbour's dinner the wine comes neat, with no water: the host is showing off his Falernian. Anyone who waters it down is loudly called a yokel.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.1.egypt: At the festival of Hathor custom says you drink until you're drunk – it is the Feast of Drunkenness. The jars never run dry before dawn, and no one counts your cups.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.2: At a neighbor's wedding the strong drink flows without measure, and the steward makes sure no cup stays full for long. Refusing here means insulting the hosts.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.3: The harvest is in, and the whole village is celebrating: jars of home brew have been carried right out into the street. The old folks are singing, the young ones are racing each other to drink, and someone is already holding out a full cup to you.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.4: Merchants are drinking to a profitable deal and wave you over to their table. The landlord brings out the strongest thing he has, and nobody keeps count of the cups.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.5: A neighbor is celebrating his new house and swears it won't stand if the guests leave on their own two feet. The cup goes round, and each guest drains it to the bottom – for the sake of strong walls.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.6: A wealthy acquaintance has brought some exotic strong drink back from distant lands and is treating everyone. According to him, it must be downed in one gulp – otherwise you won't taste it.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.7: The craftsmen of the street are holding their yearly feast and have invited you. Their custom is that anyone who doesn't finish their cup is marked as a loser for the whole year.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.8: Local men have come home from a long campaign, and the whole street is celebrating them. Each one raises a cup to fallen comrades, and not draining yours would be disrespect to the dead.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.9: Two guests have bet on which of them can outdrink the other, and now the whole feast has split into two camps. Your cup is being filled too: refusing would mean betraying your side.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.10: The new year is coming, and custom says you see the old one out so thoroughly that you don't remember greeting the new. The streets are full of songs, lights and brimming cups.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.11: An influential man with a lot of say in your life is throwing a feast and pouring for the guests himself. Setting your cup down in front of him is as good as calling him stingy to his face.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.12: The neighbors have had their firstborn, and the happy father is treating the whole street. He hugs every guest and won't let go until their cup is empty.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.13: At night at the fair, the traders sit around a fire passing a skin of strong drink from hand to hand. Custom is to drink long, while everyone around counts out loud.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.14: You ran into old acquaintances you hadn't seen in years, and the evening turned into a feast all by itself. Every story has to be washed down to the last drop – and you've got a lot of stories saved up.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.15: The rich man whose house you're visiting for the first time is showing off his stores: “You've never tasted anything this strong!” The servants never let a cup run dry, and the host watches jealously to see who drains theirs.
ev.v_wine_symposium.text.16: The local strongman won the games and is celebrating as if he'd won a war. Every guest must drink to his health, bottoms up – or he'll be offended, and offending him is risky.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.1: {npc} is getting married. You danced at the door until you were hoarse, and the next morning you couldn't remember half the songs – probably the better half.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.1.rome: {npc} is getting married. The bride was led by torchlight to the groom's house, boys scrambled for the nuts thrown by custom, and you shouted "Talassio!" with everyone else without ever learning what it means.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.1.athens: {npc} is getting married. The bride rode in a cart by torchlight, and you walked behind singing the wedding hymn until your voice gave out.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.2: {npc} is getting married. You were trusted to carry the food for the guests, and you delivered it almost intact – not counting what you sampled on the way.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.3: {npc} is getting married, and you're a guest of honor. You gave a speech you'd prepared for a week, and the only thing anyone remembers is one accidental joke.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.4: {npc} is getting married in a downpour. The guests got soaked to the skin, the musicians played under an awning, and everyone agreed that rain on a wedding day means wealth.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.5: {npc} is getting married, and the celebrations are in their third day. You don't remember which house you slept in, but you know for certain you danced better than anyone.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.6: {npc} is getting married. You stood close by through the whole ceremony and saw {g=npc_sex:his|her} hands shaking – and saw them stop when it was over.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.7: {npc} is getting married, and it fell to you to greet the guests at the gate. By evening you knew half the district by name and were hoarse from all the welcomes.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.8: {npc} is getting married – modestly, with no musicians and no grand table. Still, you've never seen your friend so happy.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.9: {npc} is getting married. You gave the couple what you could afford, and they put your gift in the place of honor – which warmed you right to the ears.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.10: {npc} is getting married. The old folks sat at the head of the table, the children under it, and you spent the evening running between the two with a jug and the latest gossip.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.11: {npc} is getting married, and by custom the guests shower the couple with grain for luck and plenty. You threw so enthusiastically that you were finding grains in your hair for a week.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.12: {npc} is getting married. Near dawn, when the guests had gone, the two of you sat on the doorstep a long time remembering how foolish you'd been when you were young.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.13: {npc} is getting married. You were so moved that you teared up right in the middle of the ceremony, and spent the rest of the evening insisting it was smoke from the hearth.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.14: {npc} is getting married. The musicians struck up the old song the two of you used to bellow down the street – and you had to sing it again, in front of everyone.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.15: {npc} is getting married. You were put in charge of keeping anyone from stealing food early, and you dutifully chased off the children – until you were caught with a flatbread in your mouth.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.16: {npc} is getting married. The torchlit procession stretched the length of the street, and you walked in the front row lighting the way and trying not to set anyone's hair on fire.
ev.a_friend_wedding.text.17: {npc} is getting married. You were seated next to the sharpest-tongued old woman in the district, and by the end of the feast you knew every local secret going back three generations.
ev.a_father_story.text.1: {npc}, your father, is telling yet again how he nearly got rich as a young man. Every year the ship in the story gets bigger and the storm more terrible.
ev.a_father_story.text.2: {npc}, your father, is remembering how as a young man he swam across the flooded river on a bet. The first time you heard it, the river was a hundred paces wide; now it's a full thousand.
ev.a_father_story.text.3: {npc}, your father, is telling how he once saw the ruler – up close, within arm's reach. You've heard this story ten times and you still nod in all the right places.
ev.a_father_story.text.4: {npc}, your father, suddenly tells you something you've never heard: how in a famine year he gave his share of bread to the neighbors' children. He says it briefly and changes the subject at once.
ev.a_father_story.text.5: {npc}, your father, is remembering his first master – how he rapped his knuckles for sloppiness and praised him once a year. “Now that was a real master,” your father sighs, and falls silent for a long while.
ev.a_father_story.text.6: {npc}, your father, tells how as a young man he ran off to see the big city and came back a week later, hungry but happy. For the first time you understand where your own restless streak comes from.
ev.a_father_story.text.7: {npc}, your father, is telling how one night he fought off a band of robbers with nothing but a stick. Every year the stick gets shorter and the robbers more numerous.
ev.a_father_story.text.8: {npc}, your father, is remembering the day you were born: the weather, who came to congratulate him, what he thought at the time. It turns out he remembers everything, down to the last detail.
ev.a_father_story.text.9: {npc}, your father, tells yet again about the terrible hailstorm of his youth – hailstones the size of pigeon eggs. Today, by his account, they were the size of hen's eggs.
ev.a_father_story.text.10: {npc}, your father, remembers an old friend with whom he dreamed, as a young man, of going to the ends of the earth. The friend left; your father stayed – and he still doesn't know whether he chose right.
ev.a_father_story.text.11: {npc}, your father, tells how he haggled with the craftiest merchant in the district and came away with three times the price. By his account, the merchant wept afterwards.
ev.a_father_story.text.12: {npc}, your father, tells of the great fire he saw as a boy: how the whole street hauled water and nobody slept until morning. His voice becomes quite different when he talks about it.
ev.a_father_story.text.13: {npc}, your father, is remembering how he taught you to walk, to count and not to bawl. You remember none of it, but you listen as if you did.
ev.a_father_story.text.14: {npc}, your father, is telling about the beast that once took to raiding their yard. At first it was a weasel, then a fox, and today it seems to have been practically a tiger.
ev.a_father_story.text.15: {npc}, your father, takes an old belt out of the chest and tells you who gave it to him and why. You never knew your father had lived such a life.
ev.a_father_story.text.16: {npc}, your father, recalls what everything cost when he was young and fumes about today's prices as though they'd been raised just to spite him.
ev.a_father_story.text.17: {npc}, your father, tells how he once got lost in the fog and walked all night toward a distant light. The light turned out to be his own home – and he still laughs about it.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.1: {npc} has taken a sleeping potion for her aching joints for years, and now she takes it with no pain at all. She dozes through the day, and by evening she is searching for the vial with shaking hands.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.2: {npc} hasn't slept at night for a long time, and one day she bought sleeping drops from an herbalist. Now the vial is always within reach, and by day she wanders the house as if in a fog, mixing up names.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.3: For a toothache {npc} started putting poppy drops in her water. The tooth was pulled long ago, but the vial still stands by her bed – and empties faster and faster.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.4: After an old friend's funeral {npc} couldn't settle, so a neighbor brought her some “calming drops.” Months have gone by, and {npc} still reaches for the vial as soon as dusk falls.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.5: {npc} worked bent double all her life, and her back has paid her back with pain. The sleeping potion helps – so well that now she takes it in the mornings and by midday can't get up.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.6: {npc} bought a “miracle cure for every ailment” from a traveling peddler – poppy drops in a pretty vial. Now she waits for his visits more eagerly than for any holiday.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.7: In winter {npc} was racked by a cough, and the healer told her to take sleeping drops at night. The cough has gone, but the drops have stayed – and she needs more and more of them just to fall asleep.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.8: You've noticed that {npc} answers at random and looks right through you. Behind the pots on the shelf you found a vial with the bitter smell of poppy – and not the first: there's a little heap of empty ones in the corner.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.9: {npc} has suffered from headaches for years, and the sleeping potion is the only thing that helps. But now she takes it without any pain: “just in case,” she says, and her hands are shaking.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.10: Money has been disappearing from the house, and for a long time you couldn't work out where. It turns out {npc} goes to the shop every week for sleeping drops and hides the vial in the chest with her festival clothes.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.11: {npc} has grown afraid of the dark and says shadows visit her at night. The sleeping drops drive the shadows away – and her along with them: by day she dozes by the hearth with a blank stare.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.12: On the neighbors' advice {npc} started taking poppy tea “for her nerves.” Now the same neighbors whisper that she sleeps on her feet, and you keep finding vials in the strangest places.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.13: Years ago {npc} broke her leg, and since then the bone has ached before bad weather. The sleeping drops were meant for rainy days – and now, it seems, for every day.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.14: {npc} has mixed up day and night: she sleeps till noon, wanders till dawn, and every evening gropes along the shelf for the vial of sleeping potion. Yesterday she knocked over a lamp and didn't even notice.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.15: {npc} keeps going to the herbalist's shop on the edge of town for “drops for a light heart” and comes home quiet and drowsy. You sniffed the vial – it smells of poppy.
ev.v_rel_mother_poppy.text.16: {npc} didn't come out for the festival: she said she had a headache and took her sleeping drops. That's the third festival in a row, and the vials on the shelf keep multiplying.
ev.f_heresy.text.1: People have appeared in town who interpret {faith} in their own way: simpler, stricter, without lavish rites and, as they put it, without corrupt clergy. You've been invited to one of their meetings.
ev.f_heresy.text.1.catholic: Wandering preachers teach that the true Church should be poor like the apostles, and that one can pray without lavish rites. You've been invited to their secret meeting.
ev.f_heresy.text.1.islamic: A Sufi brotherhood invites you to a night of dhikr: repeating the names of God for hours until your heart beats in time with them. Strict scholars eye them with suspicion.
ev.f_heresy.text.1.buddhist: A wandering monk teaches that sutras and rites are unnecessary: it is enough to repeat the name of Amida Buddha in faith, and salvation will come to anyone, even a sinner. The great monasteries are displeased.
ev.f_heresy.text.1.hindu: A wandering poet-saint sings that God loves everyone equally, the Brahmin and the poorest of the poor, and that temples and priests are not needed – only love. You've been invited to listen.
ev.f_heresy.text.2: Every evening neighbors gather at the weaver's house: she retells the old teachings of {faith} her own way and says the clergy twisted them long ago. You've been invited to come and listen.
ev.f_heresy.text.3: A priest was cast out of the temple for his bold sermons, and now he teaches right in the field outside town. He says the holy isn't in walls but in the heart, and people are flocking to him. You've been invited to listen.
ev.f_heresy.text.4: A young widow has begun to have visions and says a truth hidden from the clergy has been revealed to her. More and more people come to her night meetings – and now you've been invited too.
ev.f_heresy.text.5: A few families in the district have started living a new way: they hold all property in common, worship together without any clergy, and call wealth a snare for the soul. They've invited you to share their meal.
ev.f_heresy.text.6: A strange man in rags walks the streets teaching that the end of the world is near and only those who abandon the old rites will be saved. People laugh at him – but at night they visit him in secret. Now you've been asked along.
ev.f_heresy.text.7: People in the district have taken to worshipping in silence: no chants, no lavish rites, no clergy – only stillness. They say your heart grows light after their gatherings. You've been asked to come and sit with them.
ev.f_heresy.text.8: A wandering healer teaches that sickness is cured neither by physicians nor by rites but by true faith – and not the kind found in temples. They say he made a lame man walk. Tonight he's speaking at the miller's house, and you've been asked to come.
ev.f_heresy.text.9: A young expert in the old traditions claims that the teachings of {faith} have been misread for centuries and offers his own reading – simple and bold. His circle meets at night, and you've been invited.
ev.f_heresy.text.10: Folk from the edge of town gather in the evenings and, instead of long rites, sing simple songs about heaven's mercy. The clergy call it heresy, but the songs can already be heard on every street. You've been invited to sing along.
ev.f_heresy.text.11: New preachers teach that heaven can be pleased only by strict fasting and poverty, and that the well-fed clergy forgot this long ago. They meet in an abandoned barn, and you've been invited.
ev.f_heresy.text.12: It turns out that an old acquaintance of yours, a quiet potter, secretly leads a circle that interprets {faith} in a new way. A little embarrassed, he invites you to their meeting: “You'll understand, I know you will.”
ev.f_heresy.text.13: A wandering woman has come to town saying heaven needs neither temples nor offerings – only an honest life and kind words. Even the old folks come to hear her, and the clergy are frowning. You've been invited to her evening talk.
ev.f_heresy.text.14: Strange signs have begun appearing on walls, and soon you found out whose they were: a secret circle who believe they alone keep {faith} pure. Someone whispered to you: if you want to know the truth, come to the old well at sunset.
ev.f_heresy.text.15: Young townsfolk are outraged by the splendor of the temples and say the gold of the shrines should go to the poor. They meet in secret and are looking for kindred spirits – and they've invited you.
ev.f_heresy.text.16: Followers of a new teaching are holding a festival of their own that appears in no calendar, and they say the old festivals are empty habit. They invite you to come and see for yourself.
ev.c_child_fall.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} climbed the old tree by the road and fell. The arm is swollen and hangs wrong. {g=npc_sex:He|She} is trying very hard not to cry.
ev.c_child_fall.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} climbed onto the roof after a ball and slipped off the edge. The arm hangs limp, and {g=npc_sex:he|she} keeps asking whether anyone got the ball.
ev.c_child_fall.text.3: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} climbed into the neighbor's garden after fruit, and the branch gave way. Now the arm is swollen, the neighbor is shouting at the gate, and {npc} says nothing, biting {g=npc_sex:his|her} lip.
ev.c_child_fall.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} was running down the wet steps and slipped. {g=npc_sex:He|She} put out an arm to break the fall – and now it bends where no arm should bend.
ev.c_child_fall.text.5: The kids on the street were wrestling, and {npc} ended up at the bottom of the pile. {g=npc_sex:He|She} crawled out white-faced, holding one arm with the other, and announced, “I won.”
ev.c_child_fall.text.6: On a dare your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} walked along the top of the old wall – almost to the end. The last step went wrong, and now the arm hangs as if it belonged to someone else.
ev.c_child_fall.text.7: The rope swing on the tree by the yard went too high, and {npc} flew off it like a stone from a sling. The arm is swollen and won't obey, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} is being very brave.
ev.c_child_fall.text.8: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} was chasing the neighbor's dog and didn't see the ditch. The legs are fine, but the arm isn't: {g=npc_sex:he|she} is cradling it like a sick puppy.
ev.c_child_fall.text.9: {npc} climbed a tall tree to look at the chicks in a nest. {g=npc_sex:He|She} saw the chicks all right, but hadn't thought about getting down. The arm is swollen and hangs awkwardly.
ev.c_child_fall.text.10: The kids were jumping off a shed roof into a pile of straw, and {npc}, of course, jumped the farthest – right past the pile. The arm swelled up at once, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} proudly insists it was still the best jump.
ev.c_child_fall.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} was climbing the old ladder to the shed roof when a rung cracked. {g=npc_sex:He|She} landed on one arm and is trying not to cry, but {g=npc_sex:his|her} lips are trembling.
ev.c_child_fall.text.12: Playing tag, {npc} ran smack into the corner of a house, and the arm went crack. The game ended at once, and the other kids stand in a circle looking at you: what happens now?
ev.c_child_fall.text.13: {npc} was hopping across the stones by the river and slipped off a wet boulder. {g=npc_sex:He|She} was pulled out of the water quickly, but the arm is swollen and hangs all wrong.
ev.c_child_fall.text.14: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} was climbing over the fence, caught {g=npc_sex:his|her} clothes and went down headfirst. The clothes can be mended; the arm looks more serious.
ev.c_child_fall.text.15: In the festival crush {npc} fell, and someone trod on {g=npc_sex:his|her} arm. {g=npc_sex:He|She} walked home in silence, holding the arm carefully against {g=npc_sex:his|her} chest.
ev.c_child_fall.text.16: The kids decided to find out who was bravest, and {npc} jumped off the bank into the sand. Courage proven, arm broken: {g=npc_sex:he|she} holds it up gingerly and smiles with all {g=npc_sex:his|her} might.
ev.c_child_fall.title.5: At the Bottom of the Pile
ev.j_any_payday.text.1: The work is delivered, but the client keeps putting off payment: "any day now", "after the festival", "when the ship comes in". You've been hearing it for two months.
ev.j_any_payday.text.2: The rich man you did the work for smiles whenever you meet and promises to pay “tomorrow.” Tomorrow has lasted six weeks now, and meanwhile his house has gained a new wing.
ev.j_any_payday.text.3: The innkeeper accepted the work, praised it and asked you to wait until the travelers came through. The travelers have long since come and gone, and he just keeps spreading his hands.
ev.j_any_payday.text.4: A petty official ordered the work “for the office” and now sends you from one assistant to the next. Everyone nods, everyone sympathizes, and there's been no money for three months.
ev.j_any_payday.text.5: The neighbor you did the work for avoids your eyes when you meet and brings up his poor harvest, his sick livestock, his own debts. You almost believe him – but you have to live on something too.
ev.j_any_payday.text.6: A visiting merchant accepted your work and promised to pay as soon as he'd sold his goods. The goods are sold, and the merchant, they say, is packing up to leave any day now.
ev.j_any_payday.text.7: Your client threw a feast for the whole street, and when you came for your pay he brought you out nothing but a bowl of soup: “Not now – can't you see I have guests?”
ev.j_any_payday.text.8: Your client has suddenly started finding flaws in your work: a bit crooked here, not quite right there. He's using it all the same, but when it comes to payment he says, “Redo it first.”
ev.j_any_payday.text.9: Your client finds a new excuse not to pay every time: relatives visiting, a holiday, a bad omen. You've collected quite an assortment of his excuses by now – a pity you can't pay at the shop with them.
ev.j_any_payday.text.10: Your debtor is a respected man whose word the elders value. All the more galling that he's given you that word ten times over – and broken it every time.
ev.j_any_payday.text.11: Your client paid half and said the rest would come “later.” Two months have passed, and when you meet he acts as if you're square.
ev.j_any_payday.text.12: Your client complains of hard times and weeps over his poverty – yet yesterday you saw him buying expensive cloth at the market.
ev.j_any_payday.text.13: Your client claps you on the shoulder, praises the work in front of guests and calls you the best in the district. He's just in no hurry to pay the best in the district – two months now.
ev.j_any_payday.text.14: Once again you come to your client's house, and the servant at the gate says the master isn't in. You saw him with your own eyes in the window – he even waved at you.
ev.j_any_payday.text.15: Your client explains that he hasn't been paid himself, and as soon as he is, he'll come straight to you. The chain of debtors seems to stretch across the whole town, and you're at the very end of it.
ev.j_any_payday.text.16: The festival is coming, you need the money, and your client asks you to be patient: “After the festival, I swear!” He swore exactly the same before the last one.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.1: The young people at the gate refuse to believe that everything cost half as much in your youth, or that storms were real storms back then. You tell them anyway – and every time, the storms get wilder.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.2: The neighbors' children come running to hear how you saw a tailed star in your youth. Every time you tell it the star gets brighter and the children quieter.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.3: The young ones don't believe there was once no bridge over the river and everyone waded across. You tell them how you nearly drowned at the ford – and at last they stop laughing.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.4: In the evening by the well you tell of the famine year of your childhood. The young people listen in silence, and afterwards someone brings you a flatbread – just because.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.5: More and more often you're asked to settle how things “used to be”: where the old boundary ran, who's related to whom, when the great flood was. You remember – and feel like a living chronicle.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.6: You tell the children about the ruler who reigned when you were born. They mix him up with fairy-tale heroes, and you're no longer quite sure you aren't mixing him up too.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.7: By the gate young men are boasting of their strength, and you tell them how at their age you hauled sacks twice as heavy. They don't believe you, but they respectfully give you the spot in the shade.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.8: The children asked for something scary, and you remembered the night you got lost in the fog. By the end everyone was shrieking – you included, with delight.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.9: You tell the young folk what weddings were like in your day – a week long, the whole district invited. They sigh with envy, and you don't mention how many fights there used to be.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.10: You now have your own spot under the old tree in the square, and in the evenings people gather there to hear your tales. You've become something of a local landmark.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.11: You describe what the street looked like fifty years ago: where the baker's house stood, where the waste ground was. The young people listen as if you were talking about another country – and in a way, you are.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.12: The boys are arguing over who was stronger – warriors of old or today's – and call on you to judge. You tell them about the old days so well that the argument ends in the past's favor.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.13: You tell how as a young person you went to the great fair in a distant town. With each telling the road grows longer and the wonders of the fair more marvelous.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.14: The young folk chuckle at your old weather lore, but after you predicted rain by the ache in your knees and it really did pour, they started listening more carefully.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.15: The children ask what you were like as a child, and can't believe you were ever little. You tell them about your pranks, and they look at you with entirely different eyes.
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.16: By the gate you tell yet again about the terrible drought of your youth, when the earth cracked like old leather. The young ones exchange looks, but that evening they come back on their own: “Tell us more.”
ev.w_old_storyteller.text.17: You corrected a young storyteller who was garbling an old tale, and the whole yard turned to you. You had to tell it properly – right up until midnight.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.1: Your friends want to go and 'unwind' at the house with the lamp over its door. The madam calls from the threshold, and deep inside, behind the curtains, are girls nobody here ever asked about anything.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.2: Your friends just got paid and want to celebrate “properly” – at the house behind the market with a lamp burning over the door. The madam is already waving you over, and behind her the girls are laughing the kind of laugh that has no joy in it.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.3: At the fair your friends heard there's a “house of pleasure” nearby, and they're dragging you along. The madam on the doorstep calls every one of you handsome, and deep inside, behind a curtain, sit some very young girls.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.4: On a festival night your friends, already tipsy, decide the evening has to end at the house with the lamp. The madam greets them like old acquaintances, and the girls behind her smile wearily.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.5: An old friend is visiting, and together with the local lads he's decided to “show you how people really live.” The road leads to a house with curtained windows, where the madam is already counting the guests by heads – and by purses.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.6: Your friends lost a bet to you and, by way of revenge, want to “treat” you at the house with the lamp. The madam promises you her best girl, who stands by the wall staring at the floor.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.7: The job's done, and the older men say it's customary to “wash off the dust” at the well-known house by the town gate. The madam is already laying out cushions, the girls are waiting, and you feel uneasy.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.8: Music and laughter drift from behind a door with a red lamp. Your friends insist it's just a bit of fun, but you see the madam snap at a girl who'd stepped out for air, and the girl obediently goes back in.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.9: One of your friends is getting married soon, and the lads have decided to see off his bachelor days their own way – at the house with the lamp over the door. The madam congratulates the groom, and the girls echo her, unsmiling.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.10: A wealthy acquaintance offers to treat the whole group at “the finest house in town.” The madam bows to him almost to the ground, and the girls line up along the wall like goods on a stall.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.11: Rain has driven you and your friends under the awning of the house with the lamp, and the madam immediately invites everyone in to warm up. Your friends exchange looks, and a girl peeks out from behind a curtain, then quickly hides.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.12: Your friends are whispering that the house with the lamp has a “new girl” – brought from far away, very young. They're already heading there, the madam is calling from the doorstep, and you stand in the middle of the street not knowing what to do with your hands.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.13: The evening is dragging, and your friends suggest going to “unwind” at the house everyone knows about but nobody mentions aloud. The madam is already lighting the lamps by the door, and girls' shadows flit past the windows.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.14: In a strange town where you've come on business, your friends quickly found out where the house with the lamp is. The madam is especially warm toward visitors, and the girls greet you in silence: many of them are strangers here themselves.
ev.v_lust_brothel.text.15: A business acquaintance you're staying with is taking you and your friends to the house with the lamp: “That's how we welcome honored guests here.” He may take a refusal as an insult, and the girls behind the curtain wait in silence.
ev.f_preacher.text.1: A foreign preacher is speaking in the square. His faith is {other_faith}, and he speaks of it so warmly and simply that a crowd has gathered. Some laugh; others listen, holding their breath.
ev.f_preacher.text.2: A foreigner in dusty clothes sits by the well telling everyone who comes for water about his faith – {other_faith}. The women have forgotten their jugs, and more and more people are gathering.
ev.f_preacher.text.3: At the town gate a wanderer from far away is preaching. He has brought his faith – {other_faith} – and says it is meant for everyone. The guards no longer move him on: they're listening too.
ev.f_preacher.text.4: Under the big tree at the edge of the village a stranger is quietly telling of his faith – {other_faith}. The old folks, the children and even the headman have gathered to listen, though the headman pretends he's just resting.
ev.f_preacher.text.5: On market day a foreigner's voice cuts through the traders' shouting. His faith is {other_faith}, and he speaks so that traders leave their stalls and buyers forget to haggle.
ev.f_preacher.text.6: In the square a grey-haired foreigner leans on his staff and speaks. He has walked half the world to tell people here about his faith – {other_faith} – and they listen to him the way people listen to their elders: in silence.
ev.f_preacher.text.7: On the steps by the square stands a very young foreigner, speaking passionately, stumbling over his words, about his faith – {other_faith}. People laugh at his accent, but the crowd around him keeps growing.
ev.f_preacher.text.8: The foreigner in the square doesn't so much preach as sing – simple songs about his faith. His faith is {other_faith}, and in his songs it sounds so bright that people stop and are in no hurry to leave.
ev.f_preacher.text.9: A stranger in the square treats the poor for free and, as he works, talks about his faith – {other_faith}. The crowd around him keeps thickening: some came for healing, others for his words.
ev.f_preacher.text.10: It's raining, yet the foreigner in the square keeps talking, and people stand there with whatever they could find over their heads. His faith is {other_faith}, and it seems he'd stand in the rain till morning for its sake.
ev.f_preacher.text.11: On the riverbank where people do their washing and water their animals, a foreigner is telling of his faith – {other_faith}. Work has stopped: everyone is listening, and someone is already arguing with him at the top of their voice.
ev.f_preacher.text.12: A barefoot preacher in faded clothes has walked into town from distant lands. His faith is {other_faith}, and he speaks of it as simply as if talking about the neighbors. A crowd has already gathered.
ev.f_preacher.text.13: On a feast day, with the square packed, a foreigner climbed onto a stone and began to speak about his faith – {other_faith}. Some are pelting him with scraps; others are pushing closer to hear better.
ev.f_preacher.text.14: The foreigner speaks so quietly that people keep edging closer without noticing. His faith is {other_faith}, and he tells of it without shouting or threats, as if sharing bread.
ev.f_preacher.text.15: A visiting merchant has sold all his wares but won't leave the square: now he's talking about his faith – {other_faith}. He speaks as deftly as he traded, and the crowd around him isn't thinning.
ev.f_preacher.text.16: In the evening by the fire at the inn, a foreigner is telling travelers and locals about his faith – {other_faith}. Some snicker behind their hands; others shift closer to the fire.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.1: The one you work for left you in charge of the takings and went away for a week. The money lies in the chest, nobody has counted it, and payday is a long way off. You've also noticed your workmate already dipping into it.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.2: The owner has gone to a wedding in the next town and left you the key to the chest with the takings. There's so much in it that nobody would miss a handful – and you've seen your workmate pay the chest a visit at night already.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.3: The owner left you a chest of money for buying supplies and didn't even count it: “I trust you.” You know market prices better than he does, and your workmate is already winking: you could buy cheaper and split the difference.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.4: The owner is laid up with fever and hasn't got out of bed for a week, and he gave you the key to the chest of takings. Nobody is checking anything, and in the evenings your workmate comes back from the market with new things.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.5: The owner sent you round his debtors to put everything collected into the chest until he gets back. Only you know who paid how much, and your workmate, who collected on the next street, has clearly handed in less than he got.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.6: You've stayed behind overnight to guard the owner's property, and the chest of takings sits right in front of you. The owner's away, the lid isn't locked, and as your workmate left he patted his belt meaningfully – and it jingled.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.7: The owner has gone off to visit holy places and won't be back for at least a month. The chest of money is in your care, nobody has counted it – and your workmate is already saying heaven will forgive.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.8: Today was a day like no other – twice the usual takings, and the owner is away and only expects the usual. The chest is heavy; your workmate has already scooped out a handful for himself and is holding out a second one to you.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.9: The owner is old and half-blind; he hasn't counted his own money in years and has trusted you with the key to the chest. Your workmate laughs, “The old man won't notice” – and you know he isn't just joking.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.10: Your pay is two months late, and before leaving, the owner put you in charge of the chest of takings. Your workmate whispers that taking what you're owed isn't stealing – and it looks like he already has.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.11: The owner left for a week and, in his hurry, poured the takings into the chest without counting. Only you know how much was in it – you and your workmate, who has already lifted the lid twice when he thought you were asleep.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.12: You badly need money – a debt is weighing on you and payday is far off. The owner is away, the chest of takings is in your care, and your workmate, who has debts too, has already found a way to pay his.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.13: The festival takings were rich, and the owner has gone to stay with relatives and left the chest in your care. Nobody knows how much is really in it – except you and your workmate, who is already doing sums out loud.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.14: You haven't been in this job long, but the owner has already trusted you with the chest of takings and gone away for a week. Your workmate mocks your honesty and isn't shy about dipping his own hand in.
ev.v_theft_chance.text.15: Before leaving, the owner left the chest of money unlocked – whether absent-mindedly or on purpose, to test you. Your workmate is sure it was absent-mindedness and has already filled his purse.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.1: Word came: {npc} fell asleep drunk in the street on a freezing night and now lies in a fever. The healer says {g=npc_sex:he|she} might live, with care.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.2: Word came: {npc} got into a drunken brawl, and now the wound has festered and burns with fever. The healer says {g=npc_sex:he|she} won't get up again without care.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.3: Word came: {npc} has turned yellow, the belly is swollen, and {g=npc_sex:he|she} hasn't got up in a week. The healer shakes his head – the liver is giving out – but with good care there's still a chance.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.4: You were told that {npc} fell down the stairs drunk and cracked {g=npc_sex:his|her} head. Now {g=npc_sex:he|she} lies feverish and raving, and the healer says it all depends on care.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.5: Word came: {npc} lay drunk all night in the rain by the roadside, and now {g=npc_sex:his|her} chest rattles and the fever won't break. The healer says there's hope, if someone stays at {g=npc_sex:his|her} side.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.6: Word came: {npc} was poisoned by cheap brew – retching, feverish, eyes unable to bear the light. The healer says {g=npc_sex:he|she} can pull through, but not alone.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.7: You were told that {npc} collapsed in the middle of the market – drunk already in the morning – and has been lying in a fever in strangers' house ever since. The healer says {g=npc_sex:he|she} will live if someone takes {g=npc_sex:him|her} in and nurses {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.8: Word came: {npc} fell into the river drunk and was barely pulled out. Now {g=npc_sex:he|she} is burning with fever, and the healer says it can't be managed without proper care.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.9: Word came: {npc} tried to give up drink all at once – and now {g=npc_sex:he|she} is shaking, seeing monsters, heart racing wildly. The healer says people die of this, but with care it usually passes.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.10: The neighbors sent word: {npc} hadn't left the house for a week, and when they opened the door {g=npc_sex:he|she} was lying in a fever among empty jugs. The healer says {g=npc_sex:he|she} may live, if there's someone to care for {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.11: Word came: {npc} fell into the ditch outside the tavern one night and lay there till morning. Now {g=npc_sex:his|her} chest is on fire, and the healer says it's bad – but not hopeless.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.12: You were told that {npc} came to work drunk and got badly hurt. The wound has gone bad, fever has set in, and the healer says only good care can save {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.13: A breathless errand boy brought word: {npc} is in a very bad way – drank for weeks without eating, and now lies in a fever recognizing no one. The healer asked him to tell you: {g=npc_sex:he|she} needs care, and soon.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.14: Word came: at the festival {npc} drank for three days straight and on the fourth couldn't get up. Now {g=npc_sex:he|she} is feverish, and the healer says there's no pulling through without care.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.text.15: You've been told that {npc} lies in a fever after yet another binge and is asking for you to come. The healer says {g=npc_sex:he|she} may live if someone stays close and keeps the drink away.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink_end.title.7: In the Middle of the Market
